slides.narration: Chapter 5: Maya Math — the universe's own language. We use base ten because we have ten fingers. But the tower has no fingers. Its natural language is base phi — and it comes with a built-in engine.

lines: Base φ: uses digits 0 and 1 only
slides.narration: In base ten, we use ten digits: zero through nine. In base phi, we use only two: zero and one. Every number is written as a sum of golden-ratio powers, with no two adjacent ones — the same hard-core rule from Chapter 3.

When two adjacent ones appear, they combine and carry — eleven becomes one-zero-zero. This is because phi-one plus phi-two equals phi-three. The carry rule is the Fibonacci identity in action, and it is the engine that drives everything the tower computes.

lines: Every positive integer has exactly one
slides.narration: This representation is called Zeckendorf's theorem, named after the Belgian mathematician who proved it in 1972. Every positive integer has exactly one way to be written as a sum of non-adjacent Fibonacci numbers. The tower's arithmetic is unique.

When carries propagate through the tower, each carry triggers more carries at the next level — a cascade that turns simple local rules into complex global structure. This cascade is the mechanism behind every physical constant the framework derives. Mathematics doing itself, with no outside input.
